Reading through the comments on @MrPim's post on mustard and mayo on a Philly cheese steak got me wondering.

Is (food, but possibly more broadly applicable) taste subjective or objective? Related to the Great Steak Doneness Debate, is there any objectivity to taste at all? Does a world renowned chef hold any more credibility than the "well done plus ketchup" steak lover? If he finds nuance, balance, and depth of flavour in his sauced leather, can anyone say it's objectively a bad dish?
What can we say of the phenomenon of fine dining and top chefs if taste is entirely subjective?

It's essentially a classist popularity contest (and I say this as a food snob).

Basically it's democratically decided but your votes are weighted by how rich and cool you are. If enough ghetto trash started eating white truffles and integrating into their culture, you can bet fancy folks would abandon it in favor of something snazzier and more exclusive.

There is an objective element as people are wired to enjoy certain flavors and textures. There's also a learned component that is just based on what's locally available. But our notions of how good right, correct, or fancy a food is is due to the stuff I described previously.

What about those who prefer lower quality foods? E.g. mass-market cheese vs "artisan" cheese or supermarket bread over additive free "artisan" bread or teabag fannings over whole leaf tea.

Is this preference just a comfort thing or have they just not experienced (wilfully or otherwise) the difference?

Anyone can like what they want to. It's just socialized (within the limits of some hardwired preferences). I'd also point out that part of the reason those are "worse" is because poor people like it. You wouldn't want people to think you're a poor person, would you? You'd better be snobby and say it's crap (even when it's often fine) to signal your higher status.
Food taste is subjective, but how seriously you should take someone else’s opinion on food is objective.
